The following study, based on interviews with 52 men who engaged in suicidal behaviour, is part of an attempt to explore the background circumstances and motivations involved in the suicidal behaviour. A qualitative methodology, based on in-depth, unstructured interviews, was chosen as the most appropriate way to explore these issues. A consecutive sample of 52 men aged between eighteen and thirty years was interviewed as soon as possible after a suicidal action. All interviews were carried out by me and were tape-recorded. The tapes were later transcribed and analysed by me.

evidence.section_title: Death rather than disclosure: struggling to be a real man
evidence.quote: Non-disclosure of distress emerged as a key issue in examining pathways to suicidal action for a group of men. Disclosure of difficulties was viewed as un-masculine, as implying weakness and this was associated with feminine or homosexual type behaviour. Constant performative work, including hyper-performances, was required to project an image of strength and to conceal growing levels of distress.

The following study, based on interviews with 52 men who engaged in suicidal behaviour, is part of an attempt to explore the background circumstances and motivations involved in the suicidal behaviour.

Although there was evidence of an impulsive quality to some of the suicidal actions the men generally had been thinking about suicide for some time, often for years. Their intent in almost all cases was to end their lives and the outcome for any of them could have been death. A variety of methods were used but over-dosing with prescribed drugs was the most usual means. When they realised they were alive their reactions varied, although the majority were glad to be alive. The main reasons given by them for their actions included generalised unhappiness, being trapped in a situation, a relationship break-up, psychiatric symptoms and anger.

evidence.section_title: Performing masculinities: Being strong and concealing problems
evidence.quote: Non-disclosure emerged as a major theme in the study and was a widespread and prolonged pattern of behaviour for almost all the men. Over two thirds (67 per cent) said they would never disclose emotional matters to anyone. More specifically, almost none had spoken of the distress which led to the suicidal action. This admission was made very early in their narratives and formed an important part of their explanations around the suicidal action. It supports other research which shows the tightly controlled nature of performance around men's emotions and vulnerabilities (Frosh et al., 2002; Curtin and Linehan, 2002). As Connell (2002) remarks, the performance of hegemonic masculinity inhibits self-revelation and encourages denial of vulnerability. Non- disclosure, the failure to divulge distress to others, is therefore a key issue in examining pathways to suicidal behaviour for men. This type of performance is indicative of the emotional blockages which are part of prevailing expressions of masculinity (Whitehead, 2002; Morgan, 1992). Many men are 'unable to expose their inner selves to the outer world' due to 'fear of rejection, vulnerability, guilt, wariness or simply emotional illiteracy' (Whitehead, 2002: 157). Although this difficulty is known and has been reported on, there is little detail on its process and maintenance. As the men's narratives indicated this performance was continued, sometimes with little reflection.

Narratives often moved from subjective accounts towards more general expressions of what men usually do. Typically, subjects linked their performance to masculinity. Concealing emotions and distress, they maintained, is what men do, it is male behaviour. ; You have to be man enough to ask somebody for help, but the way people look at it, you're man enough to do it yourself, so do it yourself. Don't be asking other people for help. A man should never ask for help. ; So, being a man, appearing strong, being able to manage one's life, are important reasons for not disclosing. ; The effort involved in projecting selfsufficiency while simultaneously coping with the underlying distress often required the use of alcohol and or drugs. The result was then a spiral of concealment and denial with increasing substance misuse which compounded the initial problem. ; The consequence ofconcealing this level of distress was commonly a feeling of being trapped in an impossible situation. It led the men to a position where they felt the only way out was suicide ('it was my best option').

evidence.section_title: The confiding network: social networks and connectedness
evidence.quote: It was apparent from these men's stories that lack of disclosure around emotional difficulties was maintained even if individuals regarded themselves as having close relations with family and friends. However, other subjects detailed histories of social and psychological isolation from their own families, a separation which they themselves frequently nurtured. They often desired emotional engagement but felt unable to follow this through because an emotional discourse was unacceptable in the home and or because it went against their own expectations around masculinity.Gendered expectations around behaviour can also be shared by family and friends and this can present a further barrier to disclosure. Men can thus experience difficulties being heard when they do attempt to communicate distress. In some of the narratives it was clear that a major warning signal was ignored by family members. This reflected a deeper disconnection as some men had developed a lifestyle which was quite marginal to their families. Their objective in doing this was to create sufficient emotional distance to protect the self from unmasking. Work commitments were sometimes incorporated into this distancing operation. Social and emotional separation from wives and other partners reduced the protective possibilities ofthis environment, sometimes allowing even unusual behaviour to remain unchallenged.My whole life from the day I started work revolved around work. I loved it. For someone who spent all his teenage years or practically all of them on my own and then I went into a job where there were hundreds of people every day. When I was at school I started off as a lounge boy. If someone had said to me when I was 15 or 16 that I was going to be a barman I would have laughed at them but just one day the manager asked me did I want to become an apprentice and I said yeah. You can be in a pub with hundreds of people and yet you can still be on your own I mean from a working point of view because it is very false but I enjoyed it and I started drinking as well when I was 18 so that changed my humour to being more sociable to talk to people, not from the work front from the people I worked with. And that changed me outside work then for the better. It was years later that I drank too much. I am an alcoholic. I know. I could safely say that the first time I had a drink I was an alcoholic. I know that now but I didn't know it then. I didn't drink for the sake of drinking. I drank because it changed my humour and it made me more sociable. Of course then drinking had taken over. The reason why I was never at home most of the time was work and half of the rest of the time I was in the pub somewhere.But while family is the origin of basic trust for many, out-of-home relationships have become increasingly important in sustaining the selfin late or post modernity. Friendship was therefore another possible opportunity for the men to engage emotionally.

evidence.section_title: Men's friendships and the surveillance of emotions
evidence.quote: Friendship networks did not provide an outlet for them to express their difficulties. The opposite was often true, in that male friends were regarded as unreceptive to emotional communication. Within these narratives it was clear that men did not speak to each other about their emotions. Furthermore, any kind of confessional discourse would likely be rejected by other men. Therefore this kind of engagement was rarely attempted. Communicating psychological difficulties was regarded as 'taboo'.[/page/12/Text/2]loss or disappointment around male friendship was mentioned by two ofthe men as implicated in their suicide attempts.[/page/13/Text/2]Despite the constraints around confiding and intimacy, it was clear that the men wanted to connect to, and have friendships with, other men. Although they found some elements of friendship difficult and avoided emotional expressiveness or confiding, nevertheless, same sex friendship was for them an important affirming site for masculinity (Williams, 1992; Nardi, 2000).[/page/13/Text/2]Male friendships promote and allow expressions of loyalty, trust, and other forms of reciprocal action and support which are important to men. Such relationships affirm important elements of masculinity.

The above narratives have shown how difficult it was for the men to find emotional support and disclosing outlets within the confines of hegemonic masculinity. Yet despite the strong indications in their narratives that they did not share their emotionallives and problems with other men, they did seek emotional engagement in various ways. They found expressive outlets primarily through friendships and relationships with women but there was also some evidence of men engaging emotionally with, and caring for, each other. Yet, even in these situations they found the idea ofreciprocal friendship difficult. Emotional relationships were almost always with women but in a few instances they were with men, often men outside the family circle such as work colleagues or older men. Another confidant was a gay man. A gay man was viewed as different to 'normal' men and 'more like a woman' emotionally. Emotional discourse associated with women and gay men was therefore viewed as acceptable. One could disclose to a gay man while still keeping one's masculinity intact. Disclosing to another man was risky however - this might put one's sexual orientation into question. Gay men provided an acceptable, yet still masculine, avenue for personal disclosure. Social isolation added an additional defensive dimension to emotional concealment. What resulted was a series of barriers not only preventing disclosure but also inhibiting others from identifying the problem.

Constant performative work, including hyper-performances, was required to project this image of strength and to conceal growing levels of distress. As the men's fears and anxieties increased the opportunity for disclosure receded as the gap increased between the projected and the actual, vulnerable, self. Male friends were regarded as unreceptive to emotional communication and likely to reject confessional discourse. Communicating any psychological difficulties was regarded as taboo amongst men. The outcome is a highly rehearsed and rigid performance enacted in the face of extensive personal difficulties. avoiding confessional discourse, creating masks to disguise distress, and, not infrequently, attempting to blunt uncomfortable emotions with drink or drugs. One ofthe key obstacles in understanding men and the meaning oftheir lives is their inscrutability and their fears of emotional transparency.
